relevance_reason: This paper reports IMPG1 variants in families with vitelliform macular dystrophy (VMD) and retinitis pigmentosa, and includes a medaka model. This is directly relevant to VMD4, which is caused by IMPG1.

findings.statement: Olivier et al. (2021) performed exome sequencing in a family with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa and identified a splice variant in the IMPG1 gene. The same variant was then found in individuals from 2 more families, who had either RP or vitelliform macular dystrophy (VMD).
quotes: Exome sequencing of a family with RP revealed a splice variant in IMPG1. Subsequently, the same variant was identified in individuals from two families with either RP or VMD.

findings.statement: Olivier et al. (2021) used gene panel testing and exome sequencing to screen 596 families with RP or VMD. They identified 8 more families carrying different missense or nonsense variants in IMPG1. The authors concluded that monoallelic or biallelic IMPG1 variants are associated with RP.
quotes: Gene panel testing and exome sequencing were performed in 596 RP and VMD families to identified additional IMPG1 variants.
A retrospective study of patients with RP or VMD revealed eight additional families with different missense or nonsense variants in IMPG1.
This study discusses a previously unreported association between monoallelic or biallelic IMPG1 variants and RP.

findings.statement: Olivier et al. (2021) revised the clinical diagnosis for an IMPG1 retinopathy-associated variant that had originally been described as benign concentric annular macular dystrophy. They reclassified it as RP with early macular involvement.
quotes: the clinical diagnosis of the IMPG1 retinopathy-associated variant, originally described as benign concentric annular macular dystrophy, was also revised to RP with early macular involvement.

phenotypes.text: retinitis pigmentosa with early macular involvement

findings.statement: Olivier et al. (2021) knocked down Impg1 and its paralog Impg2 in medaka fish using morpholinos. The fish showed a phenotype consistent with that seen in the families, including shorter rod and cone photoreceptor outer segments.
quotes: Using morpholino-mediated ablation of Impg1 and its paralog Impg2 in medaka fish, we confirmed a phenotype consistent with that observed in the families, including a decreased length of rod and cone photoreceptor outer segments.

relevance_reason: Single case report of early-onset outer retinal disruption/vitelliform-like phenotype in a patient heterozygous for IMPG1 p.Leu154Pro, a mutation implicated in VMD4.

findings.statement: Gupta et al. (2021) described a 25-year-old woman with symptomatic scotoma and decreased vision who had small yellow spots at the fovea in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography showed disorganized foveal ellipsoid and interdigitation zones with reduced reflectance, worse in the left eye than the right. Fundus autofluorescence showed little, dye angiography showed nothing abnormal, and multifocal electroretinogram showed slightly reduced sensitivity in the central retina of the left eye.
quotes: We describe a case of a 25-year-old female patient with symptomatic scotoma and vision decrease who exhibited bilateral small foveal yellow spots.
Optical coherence tomography revealed disorganization and decreased reflectance of the foveal ellipsoid and interdigitation zones in the left eye more than in the right eye.
Multifocal electroretinogram revealed slightly decreased retinal sensitivity in the central retina of the left eye.

phenotypes.text: disorganization of foveal ellipsoid and interdigitation zones
decreased central retinal sensitivity on multifocal ERG

findings.statement: In a 25-year-old woman with early-onset symptomatic outer retinal disruption, Gupta et al. (2021) found a heterozygous p.Leu154Pro mutation in the IMPG1 gene by genetic testing. This mutation had previously been implicated in adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy. The authors concluded that the mutation may cause symptomatic outer retinal disturbance in the heterozygous state and said further studies were needed.
quotes: Genetic testing identified a heterozygous p.Leu154Pro mutation in the IMPG1 gene.
The p.Leu154Pro IMPG1 mutation may cause symptomatic outer retinal disturbance in the heterozygous state. Further studies are necessary.

relevance_reason: Reports novel IMPG1 mutations (heterozygous missense and homozygous splice) in patients with vitelliform macular dystrophy, with clinical, imaging and in vitro splicing data; also IMPG2 VMD cases relevant for heterogeneity.

findings.statement: Brandl et al. (2017) screened IMPG1 and IMPG2 in 106 unrelated patients with Best disease or adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy (VMD) who were negative for BEST1 and PRPH2 mutations, and identified IMPG1 mutations in 2 simplex cases with onset in early childhood.
quotes: We therefore performed a mutational screen in a cohort of 106 BEST1/PRPH2-negative VMD patients in two genes encoding secreted interphotoreceptor matrix proteoglycans-1 and -2 (IMPG1 and IMPG2).

We identified two novel mutations in IMPG1 in two simplex VMD cases with disease onset in their early childhood, a heterozygous p.(Leu238Pro) missense mutation and a homozygous c.807 + 5G > A splice site mutation.

findings.statement: In a German boy (patient 1, family 13-501) with VMD, Brandl et al. (2017) identified a heterozygous c.713T-C transition in exon 7 of IMPG1, resulting in a leu238-to-pro (L238P) substitution in the SEA I domain, predicted pathogenic by all 3 in silico algorithms and absent from ExAC. He was the only affected family member; parental data were unavailable. The authors noted that a different substitution at the same residue (L238R) had previously been reported in autosomal dominant VMD and suggested a dominant-negative effect or haploinsufficiency.
quotes: Patient #1 of the German family 13-501 carries a heterozygous c.713T > C nucleotide change in exon 7 of the IMPG1 gene that leads to a p.(Leu238Pro) amino acid substitution in the SEA I domain (Sperm protein, Enterokinase and Agrin) of the IMPG1 protein and is predicted to be pathogenic by all three algorithms used in the in silico analysis.
Patient #1 is the only affected member in the family. Data on ophthalmological examination or genetic testing of the parents of patient #1 were not available.

Thus, the current finding of a second missense mutation affecting amino acid p.(Leu238) in a patient with VMD supports the causative role of defective IMPG1 molecules in disease via an as yet unknown dominant-negative effect or haploinsufficiency.

findings.statement: Brandl et al. (2017) reported that the German boy with heterozygous IMPG1 L238P had reduced visual acuity (0.2 and 0.1 logMAR) at age 13, with central RPE abnormalities and foveal detachment in both fundi; initial diagnosis was at age 12.
quotes: At the age of 13, patient #1 showed reduced visual acuity with 0.2 and 0.1 logMAR on the right and left eye, respectively. The fundus of both eyes revealed central RPE abnormalities with foveal detachment (images not available).

findings.statement: In a boy (patient 2) from a consanguineous Turkish family (11-151) with VMD, Brandl et al. (2017) identified a homozygous c.807+5G-A splice site mutation in intron 7 of IMPG1; both parents were heterozygous. In a minigene assay in HEK293 cells, the mutation caused skipping of exon 7 in about half of transcripts, predicted to lead to nonsense-mediated decay. The heterozygous parents (aged 35 and 40) were asymptomatic with normal multimodal retinal imaging; the authors suggested that the residual correctly spliced transcript is sufficient to prevent subclinical abnormalities in carriers.
quotes: A second IMPG1 mutation, c.807 + 5G > A, was found in patient #2 of the consanguineous Turkish family 11-151 in a homozygous state (Table 1). Homozygosity was confirmed by segregation analysis in the genomic DNA of the parents.
exon 7 was skipped in about half of the transcripts leading to a 194 bp as well as the 335 bp reverse transcription (RT)-PCR product amplified in controls (Figure 1).

Our finding that a significant fraction of pre-mRNAs harboring the c.807 + 5G > A mutation are correctly spliced suggests that the level of functional IMPG1 is sufficient to prevent even subclinical abnormalities in heterozygous carriers.

findings.statement: Brandl et al. (2017) reported that the Turkish boy homozygous for IMPG1 c.807+5G-A was diagnosed with VMD at age 2 and had fluctuating visual acuity of about 0.2 logMAR over 8 years of follow-up. At age 10, mfERG was normal and EOG Arden ratio was borderline to slightly low. Fundi showed a bilateral singular central vitelliform lesion without satellite drusen; SD-OCT showed a dome-shaped foveal detachment of the neurosensory retina with hyperreflective material that was reabsorbed, leaving an optically empty cavity, elongated photoreceptor outer segments, and preserved Bruch membrane/RPE; FAF hyperfluorescence decreased over time.
quotes: Patient #2 was initially diagnosed with vitelliform macular dystrophy at the age of 2 (Table 2). During an eight year follow-up period the boy demonstrated fluctuating visual acuity of ~0.2 logMAR in both eyes.
Electrophysiology at the age of 10 revealed normal findings in mfERG and a borderline to slightly abnormally low Arden Ratio in EOG measurements (Table 2).

Hyperreflective material underneath was reabsorbed during follow-up and has left behind an optically empty cavity. Photoreceptors demonstrated an elongation of outer segments. Bruch’s membrane and RPE maintained its classical reflectivity and seemed well preserved (Figure 2B).

phenotypes.text: borderline to slightly low EOG Arden ratio

findings.statement: Brandl et al. (2017) found heterozygous IMPG2 mutations in 8 BEST1/PRPH2-negative VMD patients, including 3 stop (E226X, S522X, Q856X) and 5 missense (A243P, G1008D, F1016S, Y1042C, C1077F) mutations, the last previously associated with VMD. These patients had later onset (mean age at diagnosis 53.1 years) than the IMPG1 patients, and the authors noted that clinical symptoms tended to be more severe with IMPG1 mutations.
quotes: Furthermore, we found heterozygous mutations including three stop [p.(Glu226*), p.(Ser522*), p.(Gln856*)] and five missense mutations [p.(Ala243Pro), p.(Gly1008Asp), p.(Phe1016Ser), p.(Tyr1042Cys), p.(Cys1077Phe)] in the IMPG2 gene, one of them, p.(Cys1077Phe), previously associated with VMD.
Mean age at initial diagnosis was 53.1 years (range 33–64 years, Table 2), only one patient (#7) was younger than 45 years at initial diagnosis.
Clinical symptoms tend to be more severe for IMPG1 mutations.

findings.statement: Brandl et al. (2017) described strikingly similar phenotypes in patients with IMPG1/IMPG2 mutations, with presumably consecutive stages: singular central vitelliform lesions with neurosensory detachment and hyperreflective material above a preserved Bruch membrane/RPE; resorption leaving a dome-shaped optically empty cavity; and collapse with central atrophy and RPE loss, causing the most pronounced vision loss. All patients had bilateral singular deposits without drusen-like lesions at the posterior pole.
quotes: (i) singular vitelliform lesions in the central macula with detachment of the neurosensory retina in SD-OCT, with hyperreflective material located above the seemingly preserved Bruch’s membrane/RPE; (ii) resorption of the hyperreflective material leaving behind a dome-shaped, optically empty cavity;
(iii) collapse of the cavity and central retinal atrophy with loss of RPE. This stage of disease lead to the most pronounced loss of visual acuity.
All our patients had bilateral singular, unifocal deposits without associated drusen-like lesions at the posterior pole.

findings.statement: Brandl et al. (2017) emphasized the need for diagnostic testing of IMPG1 and IMPG2, especially in VMD patients without EOG abnormalities.
quotes: emphasizes the need to perform diagnostic testing of these genes especially in VMD patients without EOG abnormalities

relevance_reason: Reports IMPG1-mutated families with vitelliform macular dystrophy (VMD4), including the p.Leu238Arg variant, inheritance and clinical characterization.

findings.statement: Meunier et al. (2014) screened IMPG1 and IMPG2 in 49 families with vitelliform macular dystrophy negative for BEST1 and PRPH2 mutations, deletions, or rearrangements, from a French national referral center database. IMPG1 was the causal gene in 3 families (11 patients) and IMPG2 in 1 family (2 patients); the authors concluded that IMPG1 and IMPG2 account for 8% of BEST1/PRPH2-negative families.
quotes: Forty-nine families were included.
IMPG1 was the causal gene in 3 families (IMPG1 1-3, 11 patients) and IMPG2 in a fourth family (2 patients).
IMPG1 and IMPG2 are new causal genes in 8% of families negative for BEST1 and PRPH2 mutations.

findings.statement: Meunier et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.713T-G mutation in the IMPG1 gene, resulting in a leu238-to-arg (L238R) substitution, in 2 families (families 1 and 2) with autosomal dominant vitelliform macular dystrophy.
quotes: With an autosomal dominant transmission, families 1 and 2 had the c.713T→G (p.Leu238Arg) mutation in IMPG1

findings.statement: Meunier et al. (2014) observed autosomal dominant transmission of IMPG1-related vitelliform macular dystrophy in families 1 and 2, whereas family 3 was a sporadic case with presumed recessive transmission.
quotes: With an autosomal dominant transmission, families 1 and 2 had the c.713T→G (p.Leu238Arg) mutation in IMPG1
even in the sporadic case of family 3 with a presumed recessive transmission (age at onset, 38 years; mean visual acuity, 20/50)

findings.statement: Meunier et al. (2014) found that patients with IMPG1 or IMPG2 mutations had late-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy (mean age at onset 42 years) with moderate visual impairment (mean visual acuity 20/40); the sporadic presumed recessive case in family 3 had onset at 38 years and visual acuity 20/50. Drusen-like lesions adjacent to vitelliform deposits were seen in 9 of 13 patients. On SD-OCT, vitelliform material lay above a well-preserved retinal pigment epithelium of normal reflectivity at all stages, located between the ellipsoid and interdigitation lines, and electrooculogram results were normal or borderline in 9 cases.
quotes: Patients with IMPG1 or IMPG2 mutations had a late onset and moderate visual impairment (mean visual acuity, 20/40; mean age of onset, 42 years)
Drusen-like lesions adjacent to the vitelliform deposits were observed in 9 of 13 patients.

The vitelliform material was above the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) at any stage of the macular dystrophy, and this epithelium was well preserved and maintained its classical reflectivity on spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT).

findings.statement: Meunier et al. (2014) recommended screening IMPG1 and IMPG2 in adult-onset vitelliform dystrophy with moderate visual impairment, drusen-like lesions, normal RPE reflectivity on SD-OCT, and vitelliform deposits between the ellipsoid and interdigitation lines, features not observed in classical BEST1 or PRPH2 vitelliform dystrophies.
quotes: These genes should be screened in adult-onset vitelliform dystrophy with (1) moderate visual impairment, (2) drusen-like lesions, (3) normal reflectivity of the RPE line on SD-OCT, and (4) vitelliform deposits located between ellipsoid and interdigitation lines on SD-OCT.
These clinical characteristics are not observed in the classical forms of BEST1 or PRPH2 vitelliform dystrophies.

findings.statement: Meunier et al. (2014) identified a c.3230G-T (p.Cys1077Phe) mutation in IMPG2 in a fourth family with autosomal dominant vitelliform macular dystrophy (2 patients), indicating that vitelliform macular dystrophy can also be caused by IMPG2 mutation.
quotes: family 4 had the c.3230G→T (p.Cys1077Phe) mutation in IMPG2

relevance_reason: The paper is the original report showing that IMPG1 mutations cause autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive vitelliform macular dystrophy (VMD4).

findings.statement: Manes et al. (2013) described vitelliform macular dystrophies (VMD) as inherited retinal dystrophies with yellow, round deposits seen on fundus examination. These deposits occur in juvenile Best macular dystrophy and in adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy. Many cases have mutations in BEST1 or PRPH2, but the genetic cause is unknown in many affected individuals.
quotes: Vitelliform macular dystrophies (VMD) are inherited retinal dystrophies characterized by yellow, round deposits visible upon fundus examination and encountered in individuals with juvenile Best macular dystrophy (BMD) or adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy (AVMD).
Although many BMD and some AVMD cases harbor mutations in BEST1 or PRPH2, the underlying genetic cause remains unknown for many affected individuals.

findings.statement: In a large family with autosomal dominant VMD, Manes et al. (2013) used gene mapping and whole-exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.713T>G (p.Leu238Arg) mutation in the IMPG1 gene. The same mutation was then found in 2 other families with autosomal dominant VMD and the same phenotype. Structural modeling indicated that the substitution destabilizes the conserved SEA1 domain of the SPACR protein.
quotes: In a large family with autosomal-dominant VMD, gene mapping and whole-exome sequencing led to the identification of a c.713T>G (p.Leu238Arg) IMPG1 mutation, which was subsequently found in two other families with autosomal-dominant VMD and the same phenotype.
Structural modeling indicates that the p.Leu238Arg substitution destabilizes the conserved SEA1 domain of SPACR.

findings.statement: Manes et al. (2013) performed gene mapping in a large family with autosomal dominant VMD, which together with whole-exome sequencing led to the identification of an IMPG1 mutation.
quotes: In a large family with autosomal-dominant VMD, gene mapping and whole-exome sequencing led to the identification of a c.713T>G (p.Leu238Arg) IMPG1 mutation

findings.statement: Manes et al. (2013) screened 144 probands with various forms of macular dystrophy for IMPG1 mutations. In 1 family with autosomal recessive VMD, 2 affected individuals were homozygous for a splice-site mutation in IMPG1, c.807+1G>T.
quotes: Screening of 144 probands who had various forms of macular dystrophy revealed three other IMPG1 mutations.
Two individuals from one family affected by autosomal-recessive VMD were homozygous for the splice-site mutation c.807+1G>T

findings.statement: In another family identified by screening of 144 probands with macular dystrophy, Manes et al. (2013) found 2 individuals with VMD who were compound heterozygous for 2 IMPG1 mutations: c.461T>C (p.Leu154Pro) and c.1519C>T (p.Arg507*).
quotes: two from another family were compound heterozygous for the mutations c.461T>C (p.Leu154Pro) and c.1519C>T (p.Arg507(∗))

findings.statement: Manes et al. (2013) reported that most patients with IMPG1-related VMD had a normal or moderately decreased electrooculogram Arden ratio.
quotes: Most cases had a normal or moderately decreased electrooculogram Arden ratio.

phenotypes.text: normal or moderately decreased EOG Arden ratio

findings.statement: Manes et al. (2013) noted that IMPG1 encodes SPACR, a component of the extracellular matrix domains of rod and cone photoreceptors. They concluded that IMPG1 mutations cause both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive VMD, which suggested that impairment of the interphotoreceptor matrix might be a general cause of VMD.
quotes: IMPG1 encodes the SPACR protein, a component of the rod and cone photoreceptor extracellular matrix domains.
We conclude that IMPG1 mutations cause both autosomal-dominant and -recessive forms of VMD, thus indicating that impairment of the interphotoreceptor matrix might be a general cause of VMD.
